_webhook_signature_comment: How the public form's webhook is authenticated. Tally signs a submission as base64(HMAC-SHA256(secret, rawBody)) in a Tally-Signature header, over the raw JSON body and nothing else -- not a wrapper, not a re-encoding. tools/convener_ops/proposal.py::verify_signature(body, signature, secret) checks this on the GitHub Actions side; services/form-relay/src/index.js checks the same rule inside the Cloudflare Worker that receives Tally's webhook directly, before it ever reaches GitHub. `signature` is the value handed to verify_signature exactly as given (correct, wrong, or from a different body); `valid` is what verify_signature(body, signature, secret) must return. Read by tools/tests/test_proposal.py and services/form-relay/test/.

working_day_cases._comment: Working-day arithmetic, pinned across app/src/state/working-days.ts and tools/convener_ops/governance.py. Weekends are Saturday and Sunday. PUBLIC HOLIDAYS ARE DELIBERATELY NOT MODELLED: the board's members do not share one national calendar, so a holiday list right for France would be wrong for the others, and an unmodelled holiday only ever makes a window longer, which is the prudent direction. The 1 May 2026 cases below pin that as a decision rather than an oversight. The count is of the days AFTER the start day, and `elapsed` is the exact inverse of `add`.

working_day_cases._malformed_comment: Malformed input, pinned deliberately. app/src/data/validate.ts narrows every field's type and checks no date's shape, so a hand-edited 'soon' reaches these functions from the file. add_working_days answers '' and working_days_elapsed answers 0 -- an unparsable date reads as 'no deadline' and 'no time has passed', which leaves a window standing open rather than closing it on a value nothing could make sense of. JavaScript's Date accepts 2026-02-30 and year zero where date.fromisoformat raises, so those two are here by name.

_candidate_date_comment: What identifies one slot of the date negotiation: the day, and never the pair (day, hour). The question put to a speaker is whether a day suits them, the reply is recorded against the day, and the hour of the evening locked is read off the slot that day names. The two readers of data/speakers.yml disagreed about this: tools/convener_ops/validate.py de-duplicated on (date, time) while app/src/state/dates.ts keyed on date alone, so a file holding two hours on one day validated clean and then had one recorded reply marked against both -- with lockDate freezing whichever hour came first, an evening the speaker may have declined. `valid` is read by both readers (app/src/data/validate.ts, tools/convener_ops/validate.py); `answered` is what app/src/state/dates.ts must do with the slots, and says why the same-day pair is a file no reader accepts: the reply lands on the day, so both hours carry it.

_checklist_assignee_comment: Who may be named against a line of the journey. A GitHub login and nothing else: tools/convener_ops/validate.py refuses an assignee outside ^[a-zA-Z0-9-]+$, while app/src/data/validate.ts accepted any string and app/src/state/assignment.ts any non-empty trimmed one -- so the browser could write a record its own validator passes and convener-validate rejects. `''` is not in these cases: it is the answer 'nobody in particular, which is the hosts', legal on both sides and the state most lines stay in. Read by tools/tests/test_validate_v4.py and app/tests/assignment.test.ts. `assignItem` trims what a volunteer typed before applying the rule, so surrounding whitespace is not one of these cases: it is normalised on the writing side and refused on the reading one.

_lateness_comment: The overdue wording, pinned across the two languages. app/src/state/sla.ts renders these sentences on the screens and tools/convener_ops/notify.py puts the same ones in the daily digest (spec section 7): one sentence, two readers, so a reword that reaches only one side fails here. Each case carries the whole `config` the two readers take, not just `sla_days`: the board-decision step is timed by `vote_window_days` and the other three by `sla_days`, one number per deadline (F-13). The two cases with a vote window other than 14 are what makes that testable rather than merely stated: a reader that hard-coded fourteen days for the board, or read a `lead_decision` key of its own, passes every other case here and fails those two. `state` is the arm of sla.ts's Lateness; `days`, `overdue_text` and `waiting_since` exist on the overdue arm only, because a step that is not late has no day count to render. Deadlines are counted in calendar days -- the fourteen-day case spanning two weekends is here so that reads as a decision rather than an oversight.

_speaker_field_classification_comment: Which speaker field may leave the repository, and on what. Written twice -- app/src/state/consent.ts and tools/convener_ops/public_data.py -- so it is pinned here and read from both: app/tests/consent-fields.test.ts and tools/tests/test_public_data.py. The three lists are disjoint and their union is exactly the set of keys of Speaker; a field added to the model without a line here fails a test on both sides instead of reaching the public feed by omission. The argument for each placement lives in the two modules, not here.
_event_registration_encryption_comment: The wire format tools/convener_ops/eventkeys.py documents field by field (D-14): app/src/signup/encrypt.ts must reproduce it exactly, or every registration this phase encrypts becomes permanently unreadable the moment the two implementations disagree -- discovered only when someone tries to decrypt one for real. One RSA-2048 key pair, generated once for this fixture alone: never a real event's key, never touching real data, just a fixed pair so two test runners that never talk to each other still agree on it. Each case's `envelope` is the literal, unedited output of the real browser code (`encryptRegistration`, run once under Node's own crypto.subtle, which is what app/tests/signup-encrypt.test.ts itself runs under) encrypting `fields` under `public_pem` -- captured and pinned rather than recomputed, because AES-GCM draws fresh randomness every call and a recomputed envelope would never stay equal to itself. tools/tests/test_eventkeys.py decrypts each pinned `envelope` with `private_pem` through the real `eventkeys.decrypt` and checks the recovered JSON equals `fields` -- the one place that proves a browser-encrypted registration is actually readable by the job that has to read it, rather than both languages merely passing their own tests. app/tests/signup-encrypt.test.ts reads the same cases to re-encrypt `fields` fresh and check the wire shape, and to confirm the pinned `envelope` itself still has that shape.

_event_survey_response_encryption_commen: The same wire format as event_registration_encryption above -- see that key's own comment for the reasoning; this is its twin for the post-event survey (spec S:6). Reuses the identical throwaway RSA-2048 key pair rather than generating a second one: the crypto is not what differs between the two intake pages (both use the exact wire format tools/convener_ops/eventkeys.py documents), only the plaintext shape being encrypted -- so one key pair pinning both is sufficient and keeps this fixture from growing a redundant keypair. Each case's envelope is the literal, unedited output of the real browser code (encryptSurveyResponse, run once under Node's own crypto.subtle) encrypting fields under public_pem -- captured and pinned rather than recomputed, for the same reason event_registration_encryption's own envelopes are pinned rather than recomputed (AES-GCM draws fresh randomness every call). tools/tests/test_survey.py decrypts each pinned envelope with private_pem through the real eventkeys.decrypt and to_survey_response, and checks the recovered fields equal fields -- the one place that proves a browser-encrypted survey response is actually readable by the job that has to read it. app/tests/survey-encrypt.test.ts reads the same cases to re-encrypt fields fresh and check the wire shape, and to confirm the pinned envelope itself still has that shape.
